Enter cautiously — 30 ppm is well below the IDLH and is safe for short exposures
Enter and ventilate — ventilation activates automatically so entry is always safe
Enter if wearing chemical splash goggles only

1,000 lbs of ammonia onsite
Any quantity of ammonia refrigerant

questionText: A suction accumulator/surge drum in the machine room protects:

choices.text: The compressor from liquid ammonia slugs by separating liquid carryover before vapor reaches the suction
The high-pressure receiver from overpressure during defrost
The evaporative condenser from fouling
The liquid feed pumps from vapor entrainment

Natural ventilation only, without mechanical assistance

questionText: In the vapor compression cycle, the refrigerant absorbs heat from the refrigerated space during:

choices.text: Evaporation — liquid refrigerant absorbs heat and evaporates to low-pressure vapor
Condensation — high-pressure vapor releases heat to the environment
Compression — the compressor adds heat to the vapor
Expansion — the pressure drop releases heat from the refrigerant

explanation: Evaporation is the heat absorption stage. Liquid refrigerant in the evaporator absorbs heat from the product or space being cooled, changing to low-pressure vapor.

questionText: On a P-h diagram, the compression stage of the refrigeration cycle appears as:

A horizontal line at high pressure
A vertical drop from high to low pressure
A horizontal line at low pressure

Pure superheated vapor only
Pure subcooled liquid only
A region that has no physical meaning on the diagram

explanation: The vapor dome separates subcooled liquid (left), the two-phase mixture (under the dome), and superheated vapor (right) — evaporation and condensation both occur within this two-phase region.

Vapor being compressed to high pressure
High-pressure vapor releasing heat to the environment
Liquid absorbing heat and evaporating

questionText: The P-h diagram plots refrigerant properties using which two axes?

Temperature on the vertical axis, entropy on the horizontal axis
Volume on the vertical axis, pressure on the horizontal axis
Enthalpy on the vertical axis, temperature on the horizontal axis

questionText: Why do ammonia machine room detectors typically mount near the ceiling?

choices.text: Ammonia vapor is lighter than air (specific gravity 0.59) and rises — concentrations build at the ceiling first
Ammonia vapors are heavier than air and settle near the ceiling due to stratification
Ceiling mounting avoids false alarms from floor-level chemicals
Placement height does not affect detection accuracy

explanation: Ammonia's specific gravity of 0.59 means it is lighter than air and rises, accumulating at the ceiling and in roof voids — the opposite of most HFC refrigerants.

category: Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants
questionText: The primary reason industrial freezer systems use two-stage compression instead of single-stage is:

choices.text: To avoid excessively high compression ratios that cause poor efficiency and high discharge temperatures at low evaporating temperatures
Single-stage compressors are unavailable in industrial sizes
Two-stage systems use less ammonia for the same capacity
OSHA requires redundancy on all ammonia systems

explanation: Compressing from very low suction directly to condensing pressure in one stage produces compression ratios above 7:1, causing excessive discharge temperatures and poor efficiency. Two-stage compression manages this.

category: Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants
questionText: The ammonia IDLH (Immediately Dangerous to Life and Health) concentration is:

25 ppm

questionText: Ammonia's high latent heat of vaporization (~561 BTU/lb at 5°F, versus ~82 BTU/lb for R-134a) means an ammonia system:

choices.text: Circulates roughly 7× less refrigerant mass for the same cooling duty, enabling smaller pipes and lower pumping costs
Requires more refrigerant mass for the same cooling duty
Circulates the same mass as an R-134a system regardless of latent heat
Requires larger pipes than an equivalent R-134a system

explanation: Higher latent heat means more BTUs absorbed per pound of refrigerant. For the same cooling load, an ammonia system circulates far less mass, enabling smaller pipes and lower pumping energy.
referenceBookSection: Module 2 — Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants

questionText: A flash intercooler in a two-stage system functions by:

Injecting oil directly into the discharge line
Mixing high-stage and low-stage refrigerant into a single circuit permanently
Bypassing the compressor entirely during light load

explanation: The flash intercooler partially flashes liquid through a float valve at intermediate pressure, cooling the intermediate-pressure gas from the low-stage compressor and subcooling the remaining liquid feeding the low side.

questionText: Two-stage compression typically improves system efficiency by approximately:

1–2%, a negligible improvement
75–90%, more than doubling efficiency
No measurable improvement — it exists purely for mechanical protection

questionText: Ammonia's flammability range in air is 15–28% by volume. What does this imply for typical machine room leaks?

Any detectable leak is an immediate fire hazard requiring evacuation
Ammonia is non-flammable under any circumstance
Ventilation increases the risk of reaching the flammable range

explanation: 15–28% by volume is an extremely high concentration — far above what a typical leak would produce in a ventilated space. Toxicity, not flammability, is the primary hazard in routine leak scenarios.

questionText: A closed-type intercooler differs from a flash intercooler in that it:

questionText: Transcritical CO2 systems operate above CO2's critical point of approximately:

questionText: A transcritical CO2 system uses a gas cooler instead of a condenser because:

choices.text: Above the critical point, CO2 cannot condense in the traditional sense
Gas coolers are always cheaper to install
CO2 does not require any heat rejection above the critical point
Gas coolers eliminate the need for a compressor

explanation: Supercritical CO2 has no distinct liquid/vapor phase transition, so a gas cooler is used to reject heat rather than a conventional condenser.
referenceBookSection: Module 2 — Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants

category: Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants
questionText: The EPA AIM Act affects industrial refrigeration by:

choices.text: Requiring an 85% reduction in HFC production and import by 2036
Banning all refrigerants except ammonia immediately
Requiring annual reporting for facilities using any refrigerant above 5 lbs
Mandating CO2 exclusively for all new industrial systems

explanation: The AIM Act phases down HFC production and import by 85% by 2036, pushing facilities toward lower-GWP alternatives like HFOs, ammonia, and CO2.
referenceBookSection: Module 2 — Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants

category: Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants
questionText: HFCs such as R-507A and R-404A are used in industrial refrigeration primarily where:

choices.text: Ammonia is not practical, such as some supermarket DCs and pharmaceutical cold chains
They are the only refrigerant option available for any industrial system
Ammonia is banned entirely by federal regulation
The facility requires zero-GWP refrigerant

explanation: HFCs fill niches where ammonia isn't practical — some supermarket distribution centers and pharmaceutical cold chain applications, for example — though they carry much higher GWP.
referenceBookSection: Module 2 — Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants

category: Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants
questionText: Ejectors and flash gas bypass are used in transcritical CO2 systems to:

choices.text: Improve efficiency, especially at high ambient temperatures
Eliminate the need for a compressor entirely
Replace the gas cooler function
Reduce the required refrigerant charge to zero

explanation: Transcritical CO2 systems suffer efficiency penalties at high ambient temperatures; ejectors and flash gas bypass techniques help recover some of that lost efficiency.
referenceBookSection: Module 2 — Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants

category: Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants
questionText: Why is knowledge of both ammonia and HFC industrial systems valuable for a technician's employability?

choices.text: Many facilities operate mixed-refrigerant systems, and broader knowledge qualifies a technician for more work
HFC systems are being phased out entirely and no longer require technicians
Ammonia knowledge alone is sufficient for all industrial applications
Regulatory agencies require dual certification for any refrigeration work

explanation: Since facilities often run mixed refrigerant systems and different sub-areas may use different refrigerants, broad knowledge across ammonia and HFC systems maximizes a technician's employment options.
referenceBookSection: Module 2 — Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants

category: Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants
questionText: CO2 (R-744) is described as the fastest-growing industrial refrigerant primarily because:

choices.text: It has zero ozone depletion potential and very low GWP, appealing for new food retail and cold storage builds
It is significantly cheaper to install than any other refrigerant option
It requires no specialized piping or components
It has replaced ammonia in all new construction

explanation: CO2's environmental profile (zero ODP, GWP = 1) makes it increasingly attractive for new builds, despite the higher-pressure equipment it requires.
referenceBookSection: Module 2 — Industrial Refrigeration Cycle — Principles and Refrigerants

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: An operator reports 'I can't smell the ammonia anymore but the detector still reads 150 ppm.' This most likely indicates:

choices.text: Olfactory fatigue — the nose has become desensitized at elevated concentrations
The detector is malfunctioning
A different gas must be present
The operator has a natural insensitivity to ammonia odor

explanation: Olfactory fatigue causes the sense of smell to diminish or disappear at elevated ammonia concentrations. Always trust the detector over your nose.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Ammonia causes respiratory damage because it:

choices.text: Is highly water-soluble and alkaline, dissolving in airway moisture to form caustic ammonium hydroxide
Displaces oxygen in the lungs by being heavier than oxygen
Chemically binds to hemoglobin, blocking oxygen transport
Is only damaging above 1,000 ppm

explanation: Ammonia's high water solubility causes it to dissolve immediately in airway moisture, forming caustic ammonium hydroxide that burns the respiratory epithelium.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Someone covered in liquid ammonia must be decontaminated by:

choices.text: Continuous water flushing for 15–20 minutes, removing contaminated clothing while flushing unless frozen to skin
Neutralizing with a mild acid solution before rinsing
Dry wiping the skin before any water contact
Soap and water wash only, without flushing

explanation: Water dilution and removal is the correct first aid — 15–20 continuous minutes. Acid neutralization is dangerous and inappropriate.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: The human nose can typically detect ammonia at:

choices.text: 5–20 ppm, below the OSHA PEL-TWA of 25 ppm
300 ppm and above only
0.1 ppm, an extremely low threshold
Ammonia has no detectable odor

explanation: The odor detection threshold (5–20 ppm) is below the PEL-TWA, making it a useful early warning — but not a reliable safety system due to olfactory fatigue at higher concentrations.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: At what concentration can even brief ammonia exposure be fatal?

choices.text: 50 ppm
100 ppm
300 ppm

explanation: At 1,700 ppm, even brief exposure is fatal. 300 ppm is the IDLH requiring immediate evacuation, while 500 ppm can cause severe lung damage within 30 minutes.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Skin contact with liquid ammonia causes:

choices.text: Frostbite in addition to chemical burns
No injury unless inhaled
Only temporary discoloration with no lasting damage
Immediate hair loss with no other effect

explanation: Liquid ammonia is extremely cold and causes frostbite on skin contact, in addition to the chemical burns caused by its caustic, alkaline nature.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: The ACGIH TLV-STEL for ammonia (15-minute short-term exposure limit) is:

choices.text: 25 ppm
300 ppm
5 ppm

explanation: The ACGIH TLV-STEL for ammonia is 25 ppm for a 15-minute exposure, matching the PEL-TWA in this case.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: For inhalation exposure to ammonia, first aid includes:

choices.text: Removing the person from the contaminated area immediately and administering oxygen if trained personnel are available
Having the person hold their breath and walk to fresh air slowly
Immediate induced vomiting
No action needed unless symptoms appear after 24 hours

explanation: Immediate removal from the contaminated area is the priority, followed by oxygen administration by trained personnel and medical attention for any significant exposure.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Why should an untrained worker never enter a contaminated area to rescue an incapacitated coworker?

choices.text: Without proper PPE, the rescuer becomes a second victim rather than helping
OSHA prohibits any rescue attempt under any circumstance
It slows down the professional rescue team's response time
The incapacitated worker is likely already deceased

explanation: Entering a hazardous atmosphere without proper PPE and training results in a second casualty rather than a successful rescue — trained responders with SCBA must perform rescues.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Moderate ammonia exposure (100–300 ppm) typically causes:

choices.text: Chemical conjunctivitis, throat burning, and chest tightness
No symptoms until concentrations exceed 1,000 ppm
Only mild skin tingling with no respiratory effect
Immediate unconsciousness in all cases

explanation: Moderate exposure produces chemical conjunctivitis, throat burning, and chest tightness — more severe than the irritation seen at low-level exposure but short of the respiratory tract burns seen at high exposure.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: An operator doing routine machine room rounds (no abnormal conditions) should wear at minimum:

choices.text: Chemical splash goggles and chemical-resistant gloves
SCBA at all times regardless of conditions
Safety glasses and standard work gloves
No PPE if the system is operating normally

explanation: Chemical splash goggles (sealed to the face) protect the eyes from vapor that safety glasses cannot block. Gloves protect against incidental contact.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: A proper SCBA positive-pressure fit check involves:

choices.text: Covering the exhalation valve and exhaling gently — the mask should pressurize and hold
Breathing normally for 30 seconds to check comfort
Covering the inhalation valve and inhaling to see if the mask collapses
Spraying ammonia at the mask seal and checking for odor

explanation: The positive-pressure check confirms the mask pressurizes and holds without leaking. The negative-pressure check (covering the inhalation valve and inhaling) is a separate, complementary test.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Emergency escape hoods (EEBDs) placed throughout an ammonia facility are intended for:

choices.text: Allowing workers to escape a contaminated area — not for rescue entry or extended work
Providing 60 minutes of air for rescue teams
Serving as a backup during normal maintenance
Substituting for SCBA at any time a worker forgets theirs

explanation: EEBDs provide only 10–15 minutes of air for escape. They are not rated for entry into or work in IDLH atmospheres, and workers must be trained before an emergency.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Facial hair in the SCBA seal area is a problem because it:

choices.text: Prevents a proper seal, invalidating SCBA protection — OSHA requires wearers to be clean-shaven in the seal area
Only reduces comfort, with no effect on protection
Is not addressed by any OSHA regulation
Only matters for supplied-air respirators, not SCBA

explanation: Facial hair breaks the mask-to-face seal, letting contaminated air bypass filtration. OSHA requires SCBA wearers to be clean-shaven where the seal contacts the face.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Open-circuit SCBA typically provides how much air duration?

choices.text: 30–60 minutes, depending on cylinder size and work rate
4–8 hours
5 minutes
Unlimited duration, since it recycles exhaled air

explanation: Open-circuit SCBA carries a compressed air cylinder providing 30–60 minutes of duration depending on cylinder size and the wearer's breathing/work rate.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: For IDLH atmospheres, OSHA requires:

choices.text: A supplied-air respirator (SAR) with SCBA escape backup
Chemical splash goggles alone
No respiratory protection if ventilation is running
An EEBD as the sole respiratory protection

explanation: IDLH atmospheres require the extra margin of safety a SAR with SCBA escape backup provides, ensuring an emergency air supply if the primary air line fails.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: A supplied-air respirator (SAR/airline respirator), compared to SCBA, provides:

choices.text: Longer duration but limits mobility since it connects to a remote air source via hose
Shorter duration than SCBA
No mobility limitation whatsoever
The same equipment as SCBA, just under a different name

explanation: SAR provides air through a hose from a remote source, allowing longer duration than a portable cylinder but limiting how far the wearer can move from the air source.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: For maintenance work with potential ammonia exposure above 25 ppm, full PPE includes:

choices.text: SCBA or SAR, full face piece, chemical splash suit or impervious apron, chemical-resistant gloves and boots
Safety glasses and a dust mask
Chemical splash goggles alone, without respiratory protection
A standard hard hat with no additional PPE

explanation: Work above 25 ppm requires full respiratory protection plus body, hand, and foot protection — a complete PPE ensemble, not just eye protection.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Why is training on EEBD use required before an emergency, not during one?

choices.text: Under stress and time pressure, an untrained worker may fail to don the device correctly and lose critical escape time
EEBDs require a certified instructor present at every use
OSHA only permits EEBD training during scheduled fire drills
EEBDs are too complex to learn in under a full workday

explanation: An emergency is the worst possible time to learn a new procedure — donning delays under stress can consume the device's limited 10–15 minute duration before the wearer even starts moving.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
questionText: Why are safety glasses insufficient for routine ammonia machine room entry?

choices.text: Ammonia vapor can reach the eyes over or around safety glasses, unlike sealed chemical splash goggles
Safety glasses are not rated for any workplace hazard
Safety glasses fog up more than goggles
There is no functional difference between safety glasses and chemical splash goggles

explanation: Chemical splash goggles seal against the face, blocking vapor from reaching the eyes — a protection level ordinary safety glasses, which leave gaps, cannot provide.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: During an ammonia release, the correct first action for a worker without emergency response training is:

choices.text: Activate the alarm and evacuate to the designated muster point
Return to the machine room to manually shut off compressors
Find and don available PPE before evacuating
Call 911 before activating the facility alarm

explanation: Non-responders must evacuate immediately. Attempting emergency actions without training and PPE results in additional casualties.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: The Emergency Shutdown (ESD) panel for an ammonia machine room must be located:

choices.text: Outside the machine room, so personnel can shut down without entering a contaminated area
Inside the machine room near the compressor panel
In the facility's main electrical room only
Adjacent to the evaporative condenser on the roof

explanation: If the room is contaminated, personnel cannot enter without proper PPE and SCBA — the exterior ESD panel allows safe shutdown without entry.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: Safety relief valves (SRVs) on ammonia vessels discharge to:

choices.text: A water diffusion tank or a vent stack above the roof — never directly to the machine room atmosphere
The suction side of the compressor
Directly to atmosphere inside the machine room
A refrigerant recovery cylinder

explanation: Discharging into the machine room would create an immediate hazardous concentration. SRVs discharge to a diffusion tank or vent stack, well away from occupied and air-intake areas.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: The OSHA PSM element requiring documented inspection and testing schedules for pressure vessels and SRVs is:

choices.text: Mechanical Integrity Program
Process Hazard Analysis
Employee Participation
Pre-Startup Safety Review

explanation: The Mechanical Integrity Program covers documented inspection and testing schedules for vessels, SRVs, detectors, and other safety systems.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: SRVs on ammonia vessels are required by ASME code to be tested and recertified typically:

choices.text: Every 5 years
Every 20 years
Only once, at initial installation
Every 6 months

explanation: Safety relief valves are typically tested and recertified on a 5-year schedule under ASME code requirements — a key part of the mechanical integrity program.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: The Process Safety Information (PSI) element of PSM includes:

choices.text: Written documentation of system design, P&ID drawings, and safety data sheets
Only employee training certificates
Financial records for the refrigeration department
Customer contact information for the facility

explanation: PSI is the written documentation base of the process — system design, P&ID drawings, and SDS sheets — that operators must know how to locate.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: Under PSM, any release, near-miss, or abnormal event must be:

choices.text: Investigated and documented, with operators submitting initial reports
Ignored unless it results in a lost-time injury
Reported only if the release exceeds the EPA RMP threshold
Handled verbally with no written record required

explanation: The Incident Investigation element of PSM requires documented investigation of any release, near-miss, or abnormal event, with operators typically submitting the initial report.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: The correct order of the emergency release response sequence begins with:

choices.text: Sound the alarm, then evacuate, then account for personnel at the muster point
Notify the EPA before any internal action
Attempt to isolate the leak before alerting anyone
Wait for the fire department to arrive before taking any action

explanation: The sequence starts with sounding the alarm, evacuating personnel, and accounting for everyone at the muster point — before trained responders take further action.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: Which agencies may need to be notified after a significant ammonia release, depending on severity?

choices.text: The fire department, LEPC, and potentially the EPA and OSHA National Response Center
Only the facility's insurance provider
No external notification is ever required for ammonia releases
Only the local water utility

explanation: Depending on quantity and severity, notification requirements can extend to the fire department, Local Emergency Planning Committee, EPA, and OSHA's National Response Center.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety
subcategory: Emergency Response and Process Safety Management
questionText: ESD actions at an ammonia facility typically include:

choices.text: Stopping compressors, closing liquid feed solenoids, closing discharge gas valves, and sounding the alarm
Only sounding an audible alarm, with no equipment-level action
Increasing compressor speed to purge the system faster
Disabling the ammonia detection system to prevent false alarms

explanation: A complete ESD sequence stops compressors, isolates sections of the system via solenoid valves, and activates the facility alarm — coordinated actions to contain and signal the event.
referenceBookSection: Module 3 — Ammonia Safety — PPE, Emergency Response, and Process Safety

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: The slide valve on a screw compressor provides:

choices.text: Infinitely variable capacity control from roughly 25% to 100% by changing the effective rotor compression path
On/off control only
Stepped capacity in 25% increments, identical to unloaders
Compression ratio adjustment independent of suction pressure

explanation: The slide valve bypasses part of the rotor length, providing continuously variable capacity, unlike the stepped control of reciprocating unloaders.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Cylinder unloaders on a reciprocating compressor reduce capacity by:

choices.text: Holding the suction valve open during compression, preventing that cylinder from doing work
Reducing crankshaft speed via a variable frequency drive
Bypassing discharge gas back to suction
Reducing piston stroke length

explanation: Unloaders hold suction valves open, so gas simply flows back out on the compression stroke — removing that cylinder's contribution to capacity in a stepped fashion.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Reciprocating compressors are more tolerant than screw compressors of:

choices.text: Wet operation — some liquid carryover
High ambient temperature
Low oil pressure
Electrical voltage fluctuations

explanation: Reciprocating compressors handle some liquid carryover better than screw compressors, which are more sensitive to liquid slugging due to their rotor design.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Screw compressors, compared to reciprocating compressors, offer:

choices.text: Fewer moving parts, smoother continuous flow, and less vibration
Higher tolerance for liquid slugging
Simpler mechanical design with more valves and pistons
Lower maximum horsepower ratings across the board

explanation: With no valves or pistons, screw compressors run with continuous flow, fewer moving parts, and less vibration than reciprocating designs — though they're more liquid-sensitive.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Variable Vi (Volume Index) on a modern screw compressor allows:

choices.text: Internal adjustment of the built-in compression ratio to match changing system conditions
Direct control of evaporator temperature
Elimination of the need for an oil separator
Conversion between reciprocating and screw operation modes

explanation: Variable Vi uses an internally adjustable slide valve to change the compressor's built-in compression ratio as system suction/discharge conditions change, improving efficiency across a range of conditions.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Oil contamination in a refrigeration system evaporator will cause:

choices.text: Reduced heat transfer, since oil coats and insulates heat transfer surfaces
Improved heat transfer from added thermal mass
No measurable effect on performance
A higher evaporating temperature

explanation: Oil coating on evaporator tubes insulates them from the refrigerant, reducing heat transfer and increasing energy consumption.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Two helical rotors meshing together to compress refrigerant vapor describes:

choices.text: A screw (rotary screw) compressor
A reciprocating compressor
A centrifugal compressor
An oil separator

explanation: Screw compressors use two meshing helical rotors (male and female) that progressively compress vapor as it moves from suction to discharge.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Common industrial reciprocating compressor sizes range approximately:

choices.text: 1–5 HP
Under 10 HP

explanation: Industrial reciprocating compressors typically range from 50–1,500 HP, spanning single-cylinder units up to large multi-cylinder machines.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: The oil separator in an industrial compressor's oil system serves to:

choices.text: Separate oil from the discharge gas before it circulates through the refrigerant system
Cool the discharge gas to condensing temperature
Filter particulates from incoming suction vapor
Store backup refrigerant for emergency use

explanation: The oil separator removes oil entrained in the discharge gas, returning it to the oil reservoir rather than letting it circulate through evaporators where it degrades heat transfer.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Oil injection into a screw compressor's rotors serves what purpose(s)?

choices.text: Sealing and cooling the rotor compression process
Only lubricating the external bearing, with no role in the compression chamber
Increasing the refrigerant's latent heat capacity
Preventing the need for a discharge check valve

explanation: Injected oil seals the small clearances between the meshing rotors and absorbs heat of compression, both of which are essential to screw compressor operation.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: Oil accumulation of 1/8 inch in an evaporator tube reduces heat transfer by approximately:

choices.text: No measurable effect

explanation: A 1/8-inch oil film insulates heat transfer surfaces, reducing heat transfer by approximately 20% — a significant efficiency loss if oil recovery is neglected.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: An increasing acid number in an oil analysis report indicates:

choices.text: Refrigerant breakdown products or moisture contamination, a sign of overheating or water ingress
Normal oil aging that always increases with operating hours
Over-lubrication requiring partial draining
High compression ratio producing acid from metal wear

explanation: Acid number rises when refrigerant decomposes in the oil, usually from overheating or moisture ingress — a warning sign requiring investigation before compressor damage occurs.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: Minimum suction superheat before starting a compressor should be at least:

choices.text: 10°F, to ensure only dry vapor enters and prevent liquid slugging
0°F, since saturated suction is acceptable at startup
30°F minimum in all cases
Superheat is irrelevant at startup

explanation: Starting with at least 10°F of superheat confirms only vapor enters the compressor suction, preventing damaging liquid slugging at startup.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: Mechanical shaft seal warning signs include:

choices.text: Oil weeping at the shaft, refrigerant odor near the seal, and rising local ammonia detector readings
A drop in oil pressure only
High discharge temperature alone
No detectable symptoms until sudden catastrophic failure

explanation: A mechanical seal failure is a common source of refrigerant leaks — early signs include oil weeping, an ammonia odor near the seal, and detector readings trending upward in that area.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: The first step of a general compressor startup sequence is to:

choices.text: Verify oil level and oil pressure
Load the compressor to full capacity immediately
Close the suction service valve
Bypass the oil cooler for faster startup

explanation: Oil level and pressure must be verified before start — a compressor starting with low oil pressure or an empty crankcase experiences catastrophic bearing failure within seconds.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: Compressors should generally be started at:

choices.text: Minimum capacity, loading gradually as the system settles
Maximum capacity, to reach setpoint faster
Exactly 50% capacity regardless of conditions
Whatever capacity the slide valve happened to be at when last shut down

explanation: Starting at minimum capacity (unloaders off / slide valve at minimum) reduces mechanical and electrical startup stress, with capacity ramped up gradually.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: Ammonia and most compressor oils are:

choices.text: Not miscible — they do not mix well and tend to separate
Fully miscible, staying evenly mixed throughout the system
Chemically identical, requiring no oil recovery
Only miscible above 100°F

explanation: Because ammonia and oil don't mix well, oil migrates and accumulates in low points, evaporators, and vessels, requiring regular recovery.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: Oil analysis parameters worth tracking include:

choices.text: Viscosity, acid number, particulate count, and water content
Only color, since visual inspection is sufficient
Refrigerant charge weight
Ambient humidity at the time of sampling only

explanation: Viscosity change, rising acid number, particulate count (wear indicator), and water content together give a comprehensive picture of oil and compressor health.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: Regular oil recovery from low-side receivers, evaporators, and oil pots is:

choices.text: An essential routine maintenance task, since oil migrates and accumulates at low points
Unnecessary in modern systems with oil separators
Only needed once during initial system commissioning
A task exclusively performed by the equipment manufacturer

explanation: Because oil is not miscible with ammonia, it migrates through the system to low points regardless of the oil separator — regular recovery prevents efficiency loss.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
subcategory: Oil Management, Seals, and Startup Procedures
questionText: Step 6 of the compressor startup sequence — monitoring discharge temperature, pressures, oil pressure, and vibration — is performed:

choices.text: In the first minutes of operation, before loading the compressor further
Only once per shift, regardless of when the compressor started
Exclusively by the equipment manufacturer during commissioning
After the compressor has run for at least 24 hours

explanation: Close monitoring in the first minutes after start catches abnormal conditions (high vibration, high discharge temp) before they become damaging, prior to loading the compressor further.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: A vibration reading that was 0.2 in/s RMS three months ago and is now 0.6 in/s RMS indicates:

choices.text: A developing fault that warrants investigation — trend is the key indicator
Normal variation over a compressor's operating life
The measurement is likely a sensor error
Immediate emergency shutdown is required regardless of context

explanation: Trending is more diagnostic than absolute values. A 3× increase over 3 months indicates a developing fault requiring investigation before it becomes a failure.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: High discharge temperature on an oil-cooled screw compressor above 250°F indicates:

choices.text: An alarm condition — possible causes include oil cooling failure, excessive compression ratio, or insufficient superheat
Normal operation for screw compressors at full capacity
Immediate catastrophic bearing failure within minutes
A faulty temperature sensor, since 250°F is physically impossible

explanation: Normal oil-cooled screw discharge is 200–230°F. 250°F is typically the alarm setpoint, warranting investigation of oil cooling, system conditions, and valve integrity.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Vibration at 2× running speed most commonly indicates:

choices.text: Shaft or coupling misalignment
Mass imbalance of a rotating component
Rolling element bearing damage
Discharge valve leakage

explanation: 2× running speed vibration is the classic signature of misalignment. 1× indicates imbalance; high-frequency components indicate bearing defects.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Per ISO 10816 for a rigid-mounted industrial refrigeration compressor, immediate investigation is warranted above:

choices.text: 1.1 in/s RMS
0.1 in/s RMS
5.0 in/s RMS
There is no ISO 10816 guidance for this equipment class

explanation: ISO 10816 guidelines suggest investigation above 0.4 in/s, planning maintenance above 0.7 in/s, and immediate investigation above 1.1 in/s for rigidly mounted machines.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Normal discharge temperature for an ammonia screw compressor with oil cooling is typically:
explanation: 200–230°F is normal for an oil-cooled screw compressor; 240°F is a warning, 250°F an alarm, and 260°F typically triggers shutdown.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Vibration monitoring is valuable primarily because it:

choices.text: Provides an early warning tool that reveals developing faults before catastrophic failure
Directly measures oil viscosity
Replaces the need for discharge temperature monitoring
Is only useful after a compressor has already failed

explanation: Every rotating machine has a characteristic vibration signature; changes in that signature reveal developing faults well before they become catastrophic failures.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: The weekly preventive maintenance tasks for industrial compressors include:

choices.text: Checking oil level, inspecting for oil or refrigerant leaks, and reviewing trending data
A full major overhaul with bearing replacement
Sending an oil sample for laboratory analysis
Testing the HP cutout and oil pressure safety controls

explanation: Weekly tasks include oil level checks, leak inspection, and trend review — lighter than monthly oil sampling or annual safety control testing, which run on longer intervals.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: High-frequency vibration components on a compressor most commonly point to:

choices.text: Bearing damage, which produces high-frequency components before catastrophic failure
Mass imbalance
Shaft misalignment
Normal operation with no diagnostic significance

explanation: Bearing damage produces distinctive high-frequency vibration components that appear well before the bearing actually fails, making this a valuable early warning sign.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: Annual preventive maintenance items for industrial compressors typically include:

choices.text: Coupling inspection, oil strainer/filter cleaning, safety control testing, and shaft seal inspection
Only a visual walk-around with no testing
Daily operating log review exclusively
Full bearing replacement regardless of condition

explanation: Annual maintenance covers deeper inspection items — coupling, filters, safety controls, and shaft seal — beyond the daily/weekly/monthly routine checks.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance
questionText: The daily operating log for an industrial compressor should include:

choices.text: Suction/discharge pressure, discharge temperature, oil pressure, oil level, and vibration
Only whether the compressor is running or off
Annual maintenance history exclusively
Employee attendance records

explanation: Daily logs capture the core operating parameters that, when reviewed over time, reveal trends and catch developing problems early.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Industrial Compressors — Types, Operation, and Maintenance

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: An evaporative condenser is more efficient than an air-cooled condenser because:

choices.text: It uses water evaporation to remove latent heat, approaching the wet-bulb temperature rather than dry-bulb
It uses larger fans that move more air over the coil
It adds refrigerant subcooling by flooding the coil with cold water
It is always installed closer to the compressor

explanation: Evaporative cooling approaches the wet-bulb temperature, which is always lower than dry-bulb — meaning lower condensing pressure and less compressor work.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Legionella bacteria is a concern in evaporative condenser water systems because:

choices.text: The warm, wet, nutrient-rich water provides ideal growth conditions, and aerosols can carry it via the fan system
Legionella contaminates the refrigerant directly
Legionella causes scale buildup
Legionella is only a concern in potable water systems

explanation: Warm, aerosolized, recirculating water is ideal for Legionella growth. Inhaling aerosolized droplets can cause Legionnaires' disease, a severe pneumonia.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Total heat of rejection in an ammonia system equals refrigerating capacity plus:

choices.text: Heat of compression, totaling approximately 120–125% of the refrigerating capacity
Only the ambient heat load, unrelated to compressor work
Zero additional heat — the condenser rejects exactly the refrigerating capacity
50% additional heat regardless of operating conditions

explanation: The condenser must reject the heat absorbed in the evaporator plus the heat added by compression, typically totaling 120–125% of the refrigerating capacity for ammonia systems.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: High condensing pressure (above design) in an industrial refrigeration system causes:

choices.text: Increased compressor power consumption and possible high-pressure cutout
Lower compressor discharge temperature
Faster refrigeration of product
Reduced water treatment requirements

explanation: Compressor power rises significantly with condensing pressure — the pressure lift between suction and discharge directly drives compressor work, and can trip the HP cutout.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Water treatment program elements for evaporative condensers include:

choices.text: Chemical scale inhibitors, biocides, corrosion inhibitors, and blowdown
Only periodic full water replacement
Adding refrigerant directly to the water loop
Increasing fan speed to reduce mineral concentration

explanation: A complete water treatment program addresses scale, biological growth (Legionella), corrosion, and mineral concentration via controlled blowdown and makeup water.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Winterization options for evaporative condensers when ambient temperatures drop below freezing include:

choices.text: Draining the basin for dry operation, heating the basin, or using a glycol loop
Shutting the entire refrigeration system down for the season
Adding antifreeze directly to the refrigerant circuit
No winterization is needed for evaporative condensers

explanation: Freezing water in the basin or coil causes extensive damage — options include draining for dry (air-only) operation, basin heating, or a glycol intermediate loop.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Scale (calcium carbonate deposits) on evaporative condenser coils results from:

choices.text: Dissolved minerals concentrating in the recirculating water as evaporation occurs
Excess refrigerant charge in the system
Oil carryover from the compressor discharge
Ammonia reacting directly with the coil metal

explanation: As water evaporates off the coil, dissolved minerals concentrate in the remaining water and can deposit as scale, reducing heat transfer if untreated.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Blowdown in an evaporative condenser water system refers to:

choices.text: Controlled wasting of concentrated water, replaced with fresh makeup water
Purging non-condensable gases from the refrigerant circuit
A defrost method for the condenser coil
An emergency ventilation procedure

explanation: Blowdown intentionally wastes a portion of the concentrated recirculating water, diluting mineral buildup as fresh makeup water replaces it.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Undersizing a condenser relative to heat rejection duty results in:

choices.text: High condensing pressure, increased compressor power, and possible high-pressure cutout
Lower operating costs due to reduced fan energy
No operational consequence if the compressor is oversized
Improved efficiency from a more compact footprint

explanation: Condenser sizing must account for total heat rejection (refrigerating capacity plus heat of compression). Undersizing raises condensing pressure and can trip the compressor's HP cutout.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Many jurisdictions legally require which document for evaporative cooling towers and condensers?

choices.text: A Legionella water management plan
An EPA RMP regardless of refrigerant type
A DOT hazmat transport certificate
An OSHA confined space permit

explanation: Given the Legionella risk in warm, aerosolized recirculating water, many jurisdictions require documented water management plans for these systems.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Flooded evaporators are preferred over DX evaporators in industrial refrigeration because:

choices.text: Boiling liquid maintains continuous coil contact, yielding a much higher heat transfer coefficient
Flooded systems use less refrigerant overall
DX systems cannot be used with ammonia
Flooded evaporators operate at lower pressures, reducing compressor work

explanation: Continuous boiling liquid contact is more efficient than the partially wetted surfaces in DX coils, where vapor blankets insulate portions of the coil.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: A liquid recirculation rate of 4:1 means:

choices.text: 4 pounds of liquid are pumped to the evaporator for every 1 pound that evaporates
4 evaporators are served by one pump
The pump delivers 4× the evaporating temperature differential needed
The system operates at 400% of refrigerant inventory per hour

explanation: For every pound evaporated, 4 pounds of liquid are pumped to the coil, with the unevaporated 3 pounds returning to the low-pressure receiver — ensuring full coil wetting.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: The pump-down step at the beginning of a hot gas defrost cycle serves to:

choices.text: Remove liquid refrigerant from the evaporator coil before hot gas is admitted, preventing hydraulic shock
Stop the recirculation pump motor permanently during defrost
Pre-heat the evaporator to reduce total defrost time
Equalize pressure across the hot gas solenoid before it opens

explanation: Hot gas admitted into a coil full of cold liquid can cause hydraulic shock and pressure spikes. Pump-down evacuates the liquid first.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: The most common defrost method for low-temperature industrial evaporators is:

choices.text: Hot gas defrost — diverting compressor discharge gas to melt ice from inside the coil
Water defrost exclusively, for all applications
Air defrost, used at all evaporating temperatures
No defrost is required for flooded evaporators

explanation: Hot gas defrost is the most common industrial method, using diverted compressor discharge gas to melt ice from the inside of the coil.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Terminating a hot gas defrost cycle on coil temperature rather than a timer alone is preferred because:

choices.text: Temperature termination stops defrost when ice is actually gone, avoiding both short and overly long defrost cycles
Timer termination is prohibited by ASHRAE for ammonia systems
Temperature sensors are cheaper than defrost timers
Timer-based defrost only works with electric defrost, not hot gas

explanation: Ice accumulation varies with door openings, product load, and ambient conditions — a timer alone risks either leaving ice bridges or wasting energy warming product unnecessarily.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: LPR (low-pressure recirculation) pumps are typically:

choices.text: Seal-less centrifugal pumps designed for low-temperature liquid ammonia or CO2
Standard household water pumps adapted for industrial use
Positive-displacement pumps used only for oil recovery
Air compressors that pressurize the evaporator directly

explanation: LPR pumps are specialized seal-less centrifugal pumps built for handling cold liquid refrigerant safely without the leak risk a shaft seal would introduce.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Ice accumulation on a low-temperature evaporator coil causes:

choices.text: Insulation of the coil, reducing heat transfer
Improved heat transfer from added surface area
No measurable effect on performance
Automatic defrost activation with no need for periodic cycles

explanation: Ice acts as an insulator on the coil surface, reducing heat transfer and requiring periodic defrost to restore performance.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: The equalization step at the end of a hot gas defrost cycle serves to:

choices.text: Purge hot gas from the coil before re-admitting cold liquid
Increase compressor speed for a faster refrigeration ramp-up
Test the ammonia detector calibration
Bypass the low-pressure receiver entirely

explanation: Purging the hot gas before cold liquid re-enters prevents the same hydraulic shock risk that pump-down avoided at the start of the cycle.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Product stored below 32°F causes moisture to freeze on evaporator coil surfaces, requiring:

choices.text: Periodic defrost to remove ice accumulation
No specific maintenance action, since ice is self-clearing
Continuous hot gas flow with no defrost cycling
A permanent switch to DX evaporator design

explanation: Below-freezing evaporator surfaces accumulate frost from moisture in the air, requiring periodic defrost cycles to maintain heat transfer performance.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Electric defrost, as an alternative to hot gas defrost, uses:

choices.text: Electric resistance heaters in or around the coil
Water sprayed over the coil at high pressure
Compressor discharge gas exclusively
Ambient air passed through the coil at high velocity

explanation: Electric defrost relies on resistance heaters positioned in or around the coil to melt ice, as an alternative to diverting hot compressor discharge gas.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: A floating suction setpoint control strategy saves energy by:

choices.text: Raising suction pressure to the highest level that satisfies all evaporators during part-load, reducing compressor lift
Lowering suction pressure during off-peak hours
Varying setpoint based on ambient temperature alone
Reducing the number of compressors regardless of load

explanation: Every increase in suction pressure reduces compression ratio and saves energy. Floating setpoint finds the highest allowable suction that still satisfies the coldest load.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: A high-side float valve on an industrial refrigeration system maintains:

choices.text: The liquid level in the high-pressure receiver or at the evaporator inlet, metering liquid flow to the low side
The discharge gas temperature at the compressor outlet
The liquid level in the low-pressure suction accumulator
The recirculation rate of the LPR pump system

explanation: High-side float valves sense liquid level on the high-pressure side and open to feed liquid into the lower-pressure evaporator or receiver when the level rises.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: When setting minimum condensing pressure limits in a floating condensing control program, the primary concern is:

choices.text: Maintaining sufficient pressure differential across float valves, hot gas solenoids, and other pressure-dependent devices
Preventing refrigerant from freezing at low condensing pressures
Meeting OSHA minimum operating pressure requirements
Preventing condenser fans from overspeeding

explanation: Many components need a minimum pressure differential to operate — float valves need pressure to feed liquid, hot gas solenoids need differential to open reliably.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Floating suction setpoint control can reduce compressor energy consumption by approximately:

choices.text: 10–20% in facilities with variable refrigeration loads
1–2%, a negligible amount
60–70%, more than half the total energy use
No measurable savings compared to fixed setpoint

explanation: By continuously raising suction pressure to the highest acceptable value during part-load, floating setpoint control typically saves 10–20% on compressor energy in variable-load facilities.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: The operator interface for a modern industrial refrigeration PLC/controller is typically a:

choices.text: Touchscreen HMI or SCADA system showing pressures, temperatures, and equipment status
Set of mechanical dial gauges with no digital display
A paper logbook filled out by hand exclusively
A dedicated smartphone app with no on-site display

explanation: Modern systems use touchscreen HMI or SCADA interfaces to display system-wide pressures, temperatures, equipment status, and historical trends.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Hand expansion valves (HEVs) differ from float valves in that they:

choices.text: Require manual adjustment and an experienced operator to set and monitor liquid feed
Automatically maintain liquid level without any operator input
Are only used on CO2 systems, never on ammonia
Eliminate the hunting behavior seen in thermostatic expansion valves

explanation: HEVs offer a lower-cost liquid feed option but require manual adjustment and ongoing operator attention, unlike float valves that self-regulate based on liquid level.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Float valves provide liquid metering advantages over thermostatic expansion valves (TXVs) in industrial flooded systems because they:

choices.text: Meter based on liquid level, avoiding the hunting and pressure disturbances TXVs can introduce
Are cheaper to manufacture in every case
Do not require any liquid level in the evaporator
Eliminate the need for a low-pressure receiver

explanation: Float valves regulate based on level, providing stable operation without the hunting behavior that superheat-controlled TXVs can exhibit in a flooded configuration.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Floating condensing pressure control allows condensing pressure to drop at night or in cool ambient conditions. This saves energy but requires caution because:

choices.text: Some components (float valves, hot gas solenoids) need minimum operating pressure differences
Lower condensing pressure always increases refrigerant charge requirements
It voids the compressor manufacturer's warranty in all cases
It requires disabling the ammonia detection system

explanation: System-specific minimum pressure differentials must be programmed into the controller so floating condensing doesn't drop pressure below what pressure-dependent components require.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Refrigeration controllers such as those from Danfoss or Johnson Controls typically manage:

choices.text: Suction pressure setpoints, condensing pressure, defrost scheduling, alarm management, and energy optimization
Only the building's fire alarm system
HR and payroll functions for plant staff
Only manual valve positions with no automation

explanation: Dedicated refrigeration controllers coordinate the full range of operational functions — setpoints, defrost, alarms, and energy strategies — across the plant.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls
questionText: Rather than holding a fixed condensing pressure regardless of ambient conditions, a floating condensing strategy:

choices.text: Allows condensing pressure to drop as ambient wet-bulb temperature decreases, saving compressor energy
Raises condensing pressure at night to preheat the space
Locks condensing pressure at the highest historical value for safety
Has no relationship to ambient conditions

explanation: Rather than holding a high fixed condensing pressure on a cold night when the condenser could maintain a much lower pressure, floating condensing lets pressure drop and saves compressor energy.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — Heat Rejection, Evaporators, and System Controls

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: The first step in systematic troubleshooting is:

choices.text: Observe and record all operating parameters before changing anything
Change the most likely failed component immediately
Notify the facility manager before taking any action
Review the last maintenance record only

explanation: Recording all pressures, temperatures, and equipment status without changing anything first gives the full picture needed for systematic diagnosis.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: When responding to a High Discharge Pressure alarm, the first thing to check is:

choices.text: The condenser — are fans running, is water flow present, is the coil clean
Compressor discharge temperature to confirm the fault first
Refrigerant charge weight, since high pressure always means overcharge
The system log with no action until history is reviewed

explanation: High discharge pressure most commonly results from condenser problems — check the simplest, most accessible cause first before assuming a more complex fault.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: The primary reason for changing only one variable at a time during troubleshooting is:

choices.text: To isolate whether the change caused a corresponding response — multiple simultaneous changes make root cause identification impossible
OSHA prohibits multiple process changes without a written MOC in every case
Multiple changes always trip a safety shutdown
Industry practice only, as long as changes are reversible

explanation: If you change two things and the problem resolves, you don't know which change fixed it — or whether the combination is safe. One change at a time provides clear cause-and-effect.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: Consistent operating log data showing condensing pressure rising 5 psi every two weeks most likely indicates:

choices.text: Scale buildup on the condenser coil reducing heat transfer
Refrigerant overcharge accumulating in the receiver
Progressive compressor discharge valve failure
A suction-side refrigerant leak

explanation: Gradual, steady rise in condensing pressure over weeks is the classic pattern for condenser coil fouling — predictable from trending data and correctable before it becomes a crisis.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: The four-step troubleshooting approach is:

choices.text: Observe → Compare → Identify → Test
Test → Observe → Identify → Compare
Identify → Test → Observe → Compare
Compare → Test → Observe → Identify

explanation: The sequence is: observe current parameters, compare against normal baselines, identify possible causes for deviations, then test one variable at a time.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: For a Low Suction Pressure alarm, the first check should be:

choices.text: Whether the refrigerated space is already at setpoint (load reduction)
Whether the condenser fans are running
The compressor oil analysis report
The building's fire alarm panel

explanation: Low suction pressure often simply reflects light load — checking whether the space is already at setpoint is the first, simplest differential before assuming a fault.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: The 'Compare' step in systematic troubleshooting means:

choices.text: Comparing observed values against normal baselines for the same load and ambient conditions
Comparing the current fault to a list of past customer complaints
Comparing the compressor brand to a competitor's specifications
Comparing today's date to the last annual inspection

explanation: Comparing observations against what's normal for the same conditions reveals what's actually deviating — the foundation for narrowing down probable causes.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: Consistent logging is described as turning reactive maintenance into predictive maintenance because:

choices.text: Trending data reveals developing problems weeks before they cause failures
Logging eliminates the need for any physical inspection
It satisfies OSHA requirements with no operational value
It replaces the need for vibration monitoring entirely

explanation: Trend data — like a slow, steady rise in a parameter — surfaces developing problems well before they become an actual failure, shifting maintenance from reactive to predictive.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: The 'Identify' step in systematic troubleshooting involves:

choices.text: Generating a list of possible causes for each observed deviation, reasoning through the P-h diagram and system knowledge
Randomly selecting a component to replace
Calling the equipment manufacturer before any internal analysis
Shutting down the entire plant preemptively

explanation: After observing and comparing, the identify step narrows down probable causes for each deviation using the P-h diagram and system knowledge, before any change is made.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
questionText: Industrial refrigeration troubleshooting is described as:

choices.text: Pattern recognition applied to a dynamic system
A purely random trial-and-error process
A task that requires no baseline data
Only relevant after a complete system failure

explanation: Effective troubleshooting relies on recognizing patterns of deviation from normal operation, not random guessing — a skill built on solid system knowledge and consistent data.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
subcategory: Common Fault Diagnosis — Head, Suction, and Liquid Problems
questionText: Non-condensable gases in the refrigerant system (air, nitrogen) cause:

choices.text: High discharge pressure, since non-condensables accumulate in the condenser and reduce effective condensing area
Low discharge pressure by diluting the refrigerant vapor
Low suction pressure by occupying low-side volume
No pressure change of any kind

explanation: Non-condensables don't condense at normal condensing conditions and accumulate in the high side, taking up space and raising head pressure — they must be vented from the system.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
subcategory: Common Fault Diagnosis — Head, Suction, and Liquid Problems
questionText: Frost on the compressor suction flange during operation indicates:

choices.text: Liquid refrigerant is entering the compressor suction — an immediate liquid slugging risk
Optimal low-temperature operation, requiring no action
Slightly lower than normal suction pressure, expected during heavy load
Suction line insulation damage only

explanation: Frost at the suction flange means the line is at or below the frost point, only possible when liquid refrigerant is present — an immediate liquid slugging risk requiring investigation.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
subcategory: Common Fault Diagnosis — Head, Suction, and Liquid Problems
questionText: When low suction pressure is caused by a stuck-open liquid feed float valve, the symptom will also include:

choices.text: Low refrigerated space temperature and possibly frost back to the compressor
High suction superheat
High discharge temperature caused by the excess liquid
High discharge pressure from the extra liquid

explanation: A stuck-open float valve floods the evaporator, driving evaporating temperature very low — the space goes below setpoint and liquid may carry back toward the compressor.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
subcategory: Common Fault Diagnosis — Head, Suction, and Liquid Problems
questionText: High suction pressure (too warm) most commonly results from:

choices.text: Excessive refrigeration load, low refrigerant charge, or insufficient compressor capacity
Non-condensables in the high side
A stuck-open liquid feed valve
All condenser fans running simultaneously

explanation: High suction pressure means the compressor can't maintain setpoint — causes include too much heat load, insufficient refrigerant, or insufficient compressor capacity for the load.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
subcategory: Common Fault Diagnosis — Head, Suction, and Liquid Problems
questionText: Liquid slugging in a compressor is most immediately identified by:

choices.text: Banging/knocking from the compressor and frost on the suction flange near the compressor
A high discharge temperature alarm alone
A low oil pressure alarm alone
High suction superheat readings

explanation: Liquid slugging produces a characteristic knock or bang as liquid impacts valves and pistons, with simultaneous frost at the suction flange confirming liquid is entering the suction.
referenceBookSection: Module 6 — Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis

category: Troubleshooting and Systematic Fault Diagnosis
subcategory: Common Fault Diagnosis — Head, Suction, and Liquid Problems
questionText: Non-condensables must be removed from an ammonia system via:

choices.text: A non-condensable purger or manual vent procedure from the high-pressure receiver
Increasing compressor speed to compress them away
Adding refrigerant charge until non-condensables dissolve
There is no method to remove non-condensables once present

explanation: Non-condensables must be actively vented from the high-pressure receiver using a purger or a manual venting procedure — they don't clear on their own.
